chunks.text: Linear regression models the target as a weighted sum of input features plus a bias term. The weights are learned by minimising the mean squared error between predictions and true values.

A loss function measures how wrong the model's predictions are during training. Accuracy is an evaluation metric and is not differentiable, so it cannot be minimised directly by gradient descent. Loss and accuracy are different quantities.

Gradient descent updates parameters in the direction opposite to the gradient, scaled by the learning rate. If the learning rate is too large the updates can overshoot and diverge. On non-convex losses it may converge to a local minimum or saddle point.

Bias is error from overly simple assumptions; variance is error from sensitivity to the particular training sample. High bias leads to underfitting; high variance leads to overfitting. They are distinct sources of error.

Overfitting occurs when a model is too complex for the data: training error is low but validation error is high because it memorises noise. Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple and both training and validation error are high.

Data is split into training, validation and test sets. Hyperparameters are tuned on the validation set. The test set is used once at the end for an unbiased estimate of generalisation; tuning on it leaks information.
Training loss tends to fall as training continues, but a falling training loss does not guarantee better generalisation. Monitor validation loss and stop early when it begins to rise.

Regularisation adds a penalty on weight magnitude (L2 or L1) to the loss. It constrains model complexity and reduces variance, helping control overfitting. It does not add features or make the model more complex.

On imbalanced data accuracy can be misleading: a model that always predicts the majority class can score high accuracy. Use precision, recall and F1 score to understand performance on the minority class.
Precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are correct; recall is the fraction of actual positives that are found. F1 is their harmonic mean.

misconceptions.label: Overfitting means the model is too simple
misconceptions.statement: overfitting happens when the model is too simple, underfitting when too complex
phrases: overfitting is when the model is too simple
overfitting means the model is too simple
overfitting happens when the model is too simple
overfit because it is too simple
underfitting is when the model is too complex
underfitting happens when the model is too complex
questions: Think about a model that scores almost perfectly on training data but poorly on new data. Would you call its capacity small or large for that dataset?
Compare the training error and validation error of an overfit model. Which one is low, and what does that suggest the model has learned?
Now try again: in your own words, which kind of model (simple or flexible) tends to memorise noise?
misconceptions.hint: Re-read {src} and compare training vs validation error.

misconceptions.label: Tuning hyperparameters on the test set
misconceptions.statement: tune hyperparameters on the test set and pick the best model using test data
phrases: choose the best model using the test set
questions: If you pick your model because it scores best on the test set, is the test score still an honest estimate of performance on unseen data? Why or why not?
Which dataset split exists specifically so you can compare settings without touching the final exam?
Rewrite your plan so that the test set is used exactly once. What would you change?
misconceptions.hint: Check {src} for the role of each data split.

misconceptions.label: Accuracy alone is always enough
misconceptions.statement: accuracy is enough to judge a classifier, high accuracy means a good model
phrases: high accuracy means the model is good
questions: Imagine 99 of 100 emails are not spam. A model that labels everything 'not spam' gets what accuracy? Is it useful for finding spam?
Which quantities tell you how well the rare class is being found?
Which metric would you report instead for a rare-disease detector, and why?

misconceptions.label: Lower training loss always means a better model
misconceptions.statement: lower training loss means a better model, train longer is always better, zero training error is perfect
phrases: low training loss means the model is good
training loss is low so the model is good
keep training until training loss is zero
questions: A student's training loss keeps falling but the loss on held-out data starts rising. Is the model still improving at what we actually care about?
Which curve should decide when to stop training?
What practical rule can you apply when that second curve turns upward?
misconceptions.hint: Review {src}: which loss curve reflects generalisation?

misconceptions.label: Bigger learning rate is always faster; GD always finds the global minimum
misconceptions.statement: a larger learning rate is always faster and gradient descent always finds the global minimum
phrases: larger learning rate is always faster
gradient descent always finds the best
increase the learning rate to converge faster
questions: Picture rolling down a valley taking giant steps. What could happen when a step is bigger than the valley's width?
If the loss surface has several valleys, does the starting point matter for where you end up?
How would you choose a learning rate when the loss starts to bounce around?
misconceptions.hint: Look at {src} for what the learning rate scales.

misconceptions.label: Regularisation makes the model more complex
misconceptions.statement: regularization adds more features and increases model complexity
phrases: regularization makes the model more complex
regularization increases the number of parameters
questions: Regularisation changes the loss function. Does it reward or discourage large weights?
If large weights are discouraged, does the model become more flexible or more constrained?
Which of bias or variance is regularisation mainly designed to reduce?
misconceptions.hint: Read {src}: what term is added to the loss?

misconceptions.label: Confusing bias with variance
misconceptions.statement: high variance means underfitting, bias and variance are the same thing
phrases: bias and variance are the same
bias and variance mean the same
variance is the same as bias
questions: If you retrain the same model on a different random sample and the predictions change a lot, which of the two errors is that describing?
Which error remains even with infinite data because the model's assumptions are too rigid?
Match each of bias and variance to underfitting or overfitting.
misconceptions.hint: Compare the two definitions side by side in {src}.

misconceptions.label: Loss and accuracy are the same thing
misconceptions.statement: loss is the same as accuracy and we minimize accuracy using gradient descent
phrases: loss and accuracy are the same
loss is the same as accuracy
questions: Gradient descent needs a smooth signal that changes a little when weights change a little. Does accuracy, which only counts right/wrong, give that?
What do we optimise during training and what do we report afterwards?
Give one example of a loss function you could differentiate.
misconceptions.hint: Check {src} for how loss differs from a metric.
